scale.description: Candidates and voters are positioned on each axis from -2 (fully pole_a) to +2 (fully pole_b); 0 = mixed/centrist on the axis. Voter weights per axis: 0 (don't care) to 2 (care a lot). Candidate scores must carry citations and a confidence level; low-confidence scores are excluded from alignment math.

axes.title: Taxes & revenue
axes.tension: Should Washington raise more revenue from high earners and wealth to fund public services, or hold the line and cut taxes?

pole_a.label: Limit & cut taxes
pole_a.description: Oppose new taxes (income, wealth, levy-cap lifts); prioritize reducing the tax burden

pole_b.label: Tax wealth to fund services
pole_b.description: Expand progressive revenue (millionaires tax, wealth tax, cap lifts) to fund public investment

axes.salience: The single most recurrent divider: LD43 senate (wealth-tax spread), LD32, LD36 senate (repeal vs architect), LD5, every levy measure, assessor race legislative agendas

axes.title: Spending & accountability
axes.tension: Is the bigger problem that government under-invests, or that it doesn't manage and audit what it already spends?

pole_a.label: Audit & restrain
pole_a.description: Oversight, audits, performance standards, and restraint before any new spending

pole_b.label: Invest & expand
pole_b.description: Expand programs and public investment as the primary lever for outcomes

axes.salience: Differentiates WITHIN parties: KCC D8 (accountability lane vs incumbent), LD32 senate (audit homelessness spending), LD33 P2, most R challengers; measures with ratchet/flexibility concerns

axes.title: Housing affordability
axes.tension: What fixes housing costs: unleashing market supply, or public investment and tenant protections?

pole_a.label: Market supply & deregulation
pole_a.description: Streamline permitting, cut red tape, let the market build; skepticism of rent regulation

pole_b.label: Public housing & tenant protections
pole_b.description: Social housing, rent stabilization, tenant right-to-counsel, public investment

axes.salience: Seattle D5 (three distinct positions), KCC D2 (social-housing levy timing), LD43 senate (rent-stabilization stringency), LD46, LD47

axes.title: Public safety & street disorder
axes.tension: Lead with enforcement and accountability, or with prevention, treatment, and non-police response?

pole_a.label: Enforcement & accountability
pole_a.description: Police staffing, prosecuting repeat offenders, mandatory treatment, clearing encampments

pole_b.label: Prevention & services
pole_b.description: Root causes, voluntary treatment, housing-first, community/non-police responders, diversion

axes.salience: Seattle D5 (sharpest), KCC D8 (three-strikes proposal), LD5 (police chief candidate), LD47, LD30; judicial races via prosecution-vs-defense formation and bail/diversion posture

axes.title: Climate & energy
axes.tension: Press forward on climate policy even when it raises costs, or prioritize energy affordability?

pole_a.label: Energy affordability first
pole_a.description: Repeal/pare back the Climate Commitment Act and gas taxes; expand all energy sources

pole_b.label: Climate action first
pole_b.description: Defend and extend carbon pricing, clean-energy transition, climate-resilient investment

axes.salience: LD36 senate (CCA architect vs repeal), LD33 P1 (eliminate CCA plank), CD9 (Basler's affordability critique), LD45 P1

axes.title: Record vs. renewal
axes.tension: Value a proven record and institutional effectiveness, or fresh perspectives and generational change?

pole_a.label: Proven record
pole_a.description: Incumbency, seniority, bills passed, institutional relationships that deliver

pole_b.label: New voices
pole_b.description: Outsider energy, generational change, lived experience over insider tenure

axes.salience: Appears in nearly every contested race; THE axis in LD37 P1, LD11 P1, CD1, CD7, and the appointment-pipeline argument in all four Supreme Court races

axes.title: Local control vs. regional consistency
axes.tension: Should decisions (zoning, schools, services) sit with the smallest local unit, or be set regionally/statewide for consistency?

pole_a.label: Local control
pole_a.description: City/parent/district control; skepticism of state mandates and regional consolidation

pole_b.label: Regional/state standards
pole_b.description: State housing mandates, regional authorities, county-level coordination

axes.salience: LD1 P2 (GMA rollback candidates), LD33 P2 (unfunded mandates), both fire-annexation measures, Covington park district

axes.title: Money & power in politics
axes.tension: How much does independence from institutional money and structural political reform matter?

pole_a.label: Work the system
pole_a.description: Coalition-building within existing party/donor structures gets results

pole_b.label: Reform the system
pole_b.description: Refuse PAC money; term limits, dark-money bans, RCV, direct democracy

axes.salience: Central for Etzkorn (CD1), Gordon, Sawant/Chaudhry (CD9), Sabio-Howell (LD43), Brown (LD37), Leritz (LD5), Jacobson (KCC D8)

axes.title: Immigration & federal enforcement
axes.tension: Constrain federal immigration enforcement and protect immigrants, or prioritize enforcement and border security?

pole_a.label: Enforcement first
pole_a.description: Secure border, support ICE cooperation, enforcement of immigration law

pole_b.label: Protect immigrants
pole_b.description: Constrain ICE (masking bans, surveillance limits), sanctuary policies, legal pathways

axes.salience: CD7 (Jayapal's signature), CD9 (abolish-ICE spread), CD8 (R field), LD32 P2 (Siddiqi), LD46 senate, LD33 P1

axes.title: Healthcare system
axes.tension: Replace private insurance with a universal public system, or strengthen and fix the current system?

pole_a.label: Strengthen current system
pole_a.description: Protect ACA/Medicaid, cap drug prices, lower premiums within existing structures

pole_b.label: Single-payer transformation
pole_b.description: Medicare for All / universal public coverage as the goal

axes.salience: CD1 (three-way split), CD7, CD9 (mechanism/urgency differences), LD5 (Warmerdam single-payer), LD1 P2

axes.title: Gender, LGBTQ+ and reproductive policy
axes.tension: Should state law protect gender identity, LGBTQ+ rights and reproductive choice broadly (in school sports, medical care and anti-discrimination law), or set traditional sex-based and pro-life limits?

pole_a.label: Traditional values
pole_a.description: Sex-based eligibility for girls' and women's sports, limits on gender-affirming care for minors, pro-life positions, narrower anti-discrimination protections

pole_b.label: Progressive social policy
pole_b.description: Trans participation in sports by gender identity, reproductive and gender-affirming care as rights, broad anti-discrimination law

axes.salience: General ballot: I-638 (sex verification for girls' school sports) maps here. Primary evidence: LD47 P2 (DEI removal vs Members of Color Caucus chair), LD45 P1, LD41 P1, LD33 P1 (three-way spread), LD12 P2, LD46 senate. Curricula and parental-rights evidence now belongs to parental-rights.

axes.title: Parents and public schools
axes.tension: Should parents have broad notification, record access and opt-out rights over what schools teach and provide, or should schools and students have discretion?

pole_a.label: Parental notification and opt-out
pole_a.description: Parents notified of and able to review curricula, materials, records and school-provided health services; broad opt-out rights

pole_b.label: School and student discretion
pole_b.description: Educators set curricula under state standards; student privacy and confidentiality in some health and counseling matters; narrower opt-outs

axes.salience: General ballot: I-1 (parental rights in schools) maps here. Applies to state legislative contests, school-district and other school-adjacent measures, and statewide initiatives; never to judicial contests. Split from social so a voter can support one of I-1 and I-638 and oppose the other.

axes.title: AI & big tech
axes.tension: Regulate AI, data centers, and tech platforms aggressively, or keep Washington innovation-friendly?

pole_a.label: Innovation-friendly
pole_a.description: Light-touch regulation; treat tech/AI growth and its energy demand as opportunity

pole_b.label: Regulate aggressively
pole_b.description: AI guardrails, data-center limits/subsidy skepticism, platform accountability, data privacy

axes.salience: The novel axis this cycle: LD46 P1 (race's flashpoint, AI-industry money contested), LD32 P1 (Noble's platform), LD32 senate, LD45 P2, CD1 (halt data centers vs nationalize AI vs opportunity)

axes.title: Foreign policy & defense
axes.tension: Reduce military spending and conditions on aid (especially to Israel), or maintain defense commitments and alliances?

pole_a.label: Maintain commitments
pole_a.description: Strong defense budget, support allies including Israel, defense-industry partnership

pole_b.label: Reduce & recondition
pole_b.description: Arms embargo/aid conditions on Israel, audit/cut the Pentagon, end forever wars

axes.salience: CD9's clearest divider (HASC ranking member vs arms-embargo challengers), CD7 (War Powers), CD1

axes.title: Judicial philosophy
axes.tension: Should judges read law strictly as written, or pragmatically interpret it to protect rights as society changes?

pole_a.label: As written
pole_a.description: Strict construction, text and original meaning, judicial restraint, depoliticize the court

pole_b.label: Pragmatic & rights-protective
pole_b.description: State constitution as rights guarantor, law meeting the community where it is, openness to reform

axes.salience: SSC Pos 3 (clearest three-way philosophy spread), Pos 1 (rights-guarantor vs as-written), Pos 5 (posture toward Blake/bail), Pos 7 (Quinn/Blake critiques); Seattle Muni Court via bail/diversion posture

interview.authored_by: Hand-authored for this ballot from data/final/2026-11-03-general/rubric.json axes; each item maps agree -> a signed axis value. Statement directions are deliberately mixed so 'agree' alternates poles across the interview (acquiescence-bias guard).
interview.notes: value semantics: agree applies `value`, disagree applies `-value`, skip applies nothing. weight from care pulse: not-much=0.5, default=1, a-lot=2. Scenarios apply every effect listed for the chosen option. General-election changes (issue #4, 2026-10-08): card-social reworded to the narrowed social axis and flipped to value 2; card-parental-rights added with value -2 so agree keeps alternating poles (healthcare -2, social +2, parental-rights -2, tech +2, defense -2).

items.text: Washington should tax high incomes and large fortunes more to fund public services.
Before asking taxpayers for anything new, government should first prove it spends what it already has well.
The county finds a budget surplus. Where should it go first?

options.label: Hiring more police officers
options.detail: Faster response times and more patrols

items.text: The fastest fix for housing costs is cutting permits and regulations so builders can build more.
Climate policies like carbon pricing are worth it, even when they raise gas and energy prices.
I'd rather have an experienced insider who knows how to get things done than a newcomer with fresh ideas.
Two housing bills reach the governor's desk, but only one gets funded. Which one?

options.label: Cut red tape for builders
options.detail: Streamlined permits, relaxed zoning — let supply catch up

options.label: Public housing & renter protections
options.detail: Social housing dollars, rent stabilization, right to counsel

items.text: Zoning and school decisions belong with each city and community — not with the state.
I trust a candidate more when they refuse PAC and corporate money.
State and local government should limit how much they cooperate with federal immigration enforcement.
Healthcare works better when we improve the system we have, rather than replacing private insurance with one public plan.
Olympia faces a budget shortfall. What should legislators reach for first?

options.label: Cut programs & find efficiencies
options.detail: Tighten belts before touching anyone's taxes

options.label: New taxes on the wealthiest
options.detail: Protect services by asking more from those with the most

items.text: State law should protect transgender people's rights, including playing on school sports teams that match their gender identity.
Parents should be able to see their child's school records and opt their child out of lessons or school services they object to.
AI companies and data centers need much stricter rules here, even if that slows the local tech economy.
The U.S. should keep supporting allies like Israel with military aid, without adding new conditions.
Judges should stick to the exact text of the law as written — even when a strict reading produces harsh results.

contests.office_does: One of nine statewide-elected justices on Washington's court of last resort, deciding appeals, state constitutional questions, and the rules that govern every court in the state.
contests.race_blurb: A race for the two years left on retired Justice Mary Yu's term. Justice Colleen Melody, appointed by Governor Ferguson and on the court since January 2026, led the August primary with 53% against tax and constitutional attorney Scott Edwards (29%), who runs on applying the law "as written" and against the appointment pipeline.

candidates.name: Colleen Melody
candidates.summary: Sitting justice since January 2026, appointed after leading the Attorney General's Civil Rights Division. She calls state law "the backbone of a lot of our rights right now" and is endorsed by every sitting justice.
highlights: On the Supreme Court since January 2026; wrote the 5-4 majority in In re Marriage of Hauk (Child Relocation Act) and joined the 6-3 majority striking the natural-gas initiative [S6][S8]
Says "State law is really the backbone of a lot of our rights right now" and names Justice Kagan as a model for attention to rulings' practical effects [S9][S10]
Also told the Seattle Times the court should "stay in its lane, and not veer into policy, unnecessarily" [S12]
Led the AG's Civil Rights Division, including the travel-ban challenge [S18]
Endorsed by all sitting justices, Governors Ferguson, Inslee and Gregoire, and the State Labor Council; first in the primary with 53.03% [S1][S14]

judicial.basis: Repeatedly frames state law and state courts as rights guarantors and cites practical effects (Kagan model); her 'stay in its lane' remark and text-based Hauk opinion keep her off the pole. Down from +2 in the primary because the refreshed record adds those moderating items.

experience.basis: Incumbent with the full institutional roster behind her, but appointed and on the bench only since January 2026 after a government litigation career; evidence unchanged in substance from the primary.

Mason County Superior Court Judge David Stevens, a self-described textualist and originalist and critic of the court's criminal-procedure rules, finished first in the August primary (35.3%) against King County Superior Court Judge Jaime Hawk (33.4%), a former public defender and ACLU attorney backed by most sitting justices and the governor.

candidates.name: David Stevens
candidates.summary: Mason County Superior Court judge, elected in 2023 over an appointed incumbent, with a career spanning state, federal and international prosecution and public defense. He describes himself as a textualist and originalist and criticizes recent Supreme Court rules on criminal procedure.
highlights: Site: the state constitution "should be interpreted based on its text and original meaning and not on evolving societal standards" [S3]
Criticizes the court's juvenile-warrant, arraignment-deadline and jury-selection rules and supports failure-to-appear warrants [S3][S10]
About a decade as a Spokane County deputy prosecutor, plus federal prosecutor and public-defender roles [S1][S8]
Argues appointment of judges "leads to ideological and political decisions"; reached the bench by defeating an appointed incumbent [S1][S4][S8]
First in the primary with 35.29%; endorsed by WACOPS and recommended by the state Republican Party [S7][S8]

judicial.basis: Self-described textualist/originalist; text-and-original-meaning reading of the constitution and 'not for the courts to lead the way'; unchanged from the primary, now with more statements.

safety.basis: Documented positions against the court's juvenile-warrant, arraignment-deadline and bail-related rule changes and for failure-to-appear warrants, on a prosecution-heavy career; public-defender years keep it off -2. Confidence raised from medium because the positions are now repeated across his site and news interviews.

experience.basis: A sitting elected trial judge who campaigns as the outsider to the appointment pipeline; unchanged from the primary.

contests.office_does: One of nine statewide-elected justices on Washington's court of last resort, deciding appeals, state constitutional questions, and the rules that govern every court in the state.
contests.race_blurb: An open seat: Justice Charles W. Johnson must retire at 75, and only two candidates filed, so the race skipped the primary. Court of Appeals Judge Ian Birk, backed by most sitting justices and labor, faces King County Superior Court Judge Sean O'Donnell, a former prosecutor backed by the Seattle Times, law enforcement, the state Republican Party and Democratic officials including Gregoire; O'Donnell's Republican recommendation and Birk's fundraising emails about it have become a point of dispute.

candidates.name: Ian Birk
candidates.summary: Division I Court of Appeals judge since a 2022 appointment, after 20 years as a civil litigator representing consumers and policyholders. He points to 200-plus appellate opinions and the backing of most sitting justices.
highlights: Court of Appeals judge since April 2022 (appointed, then retained unopposed), with more than 200 authored opinions [S6][S3]
Wrote the published opinion letting the Attorney General subpoena Archdiocese of Seattle records on clergy abuse, within religion-clause limits [S8]
Says the state constitution is "more important now than it ever has" been and that he decides cases with "respect for legal precedent" [S11][S5]
Endorsed by seven sitting justices, AG Brown, the State Labor Council and King County Democrats; rated Exceptionally Well Qualified by Washington Women Lawyers [S4][S11][S1][S17]
His campaign's emails calling O'Donnell "a Republican-affiliated judge" drew a letter from 62 judges and a Seattle Times editorial [S14][S15]

experience.basis: Sitting appellate judge with institutional support from most of the court, but four years on the bench by appointment; new candidate, first scoring.

safety.basis: In his own written questionnaire answers he reports taking a National Judicial College seminar on 'reducing disparity through nontraditional diversion' and says he intends to bring that to his work, alongside a call for judges to address the system's 'disproportionate impact on communities of color and people of limited means' [S7]. This is a single clear first-person statement favoring diversion, which the judicial safety rule accepts. Not higher, because he has no criminal-law formation and no bail or diversion rulings.

candidates.summary: Retired Federal Way Municipal Court presiding judge with 18 years on the bench and 23 as a trial lawyer, and a repeat Supreme Court candidate who lost the 2024 race by about 20,000 votes. He runs as a critic of the court's direction and the appointment process.
highlights: Site: "Apply the law as written, not as you wish it had been" [S4]
Called the Blake decision "motivated by ideology" and opposed proposed bail rules he said would "cripple" trial courts [S2]
Served on the DMCJA Therapeutic Courts Committee 2019-2025 [S6]
Proposes a bipartisan Judicial Elections Commission to vet appointees [S8][S9]
Second in the primary with 32.24%; the one located 2026 bar rating is "Qualified" (Tacoma-Pierce County Bar) [S16][S11]

judicial.basis: New campaign-site statement 'Apply the law as written, not as you wish it had been' and 'not to impose ideology', on top of the primary's Blake-was-ideological criticism. Moved from -1 to -2; medium because it rests on campaign-site wording plus one earlier interview.

safety.basis: Genuinely mixed: opposed proposed bail rules and says court decisions weakened trial courts' response to crime, yet served six years on the Therapeutic Courts Committee and campaigns on 'compassion and accountability'; unchanged from the primary.

experience.basis: Long judicial tenure (18 years, municipal level) but campaigns as an outsider against the appointed incumbent and the appointment process; unchanged from the primary.

contests.office_does: One of nine statewide-elected justices on Washington's court of last resort, deciding appeals, state constitutional questions, and the rules that govern every court in the state.
contests.race_blurb: Chief Justice Debra Stephens, on the court since 2008, led the August primary with 54.5% against Tacoma tax attorney and Navy veteran Todd Bloom (27.2%), who has never held judicial office and criticizes the court's McCleary, Quinn and natural-gas initiative rulings.

candidates.name: Debra L. Stephens
candidates.summary: Chief Justice and a justice since 2008, formerly a Court of Appeals judge and Gonzaga appellate lawyer and professor. She describes a text-and-structure method applied to a constitution written as a broad framework, and wrote McCleary.
highlights: On the court since 2008, Chief Justice since January 2025 [S1][S7]
Wrote McCleary (2012), recognizing a positive constitutional right to amply funded K-12 education [S2][S6]
Wrote the 6-3 majority striking Initiative 2066 on single-subject grounds [S4][S10]
Describes "respect for text and structure" and admires Justice Brennan's view that "rights without remedies are hollow" [S9]
Endorsed by all other sitting justices and 150+ judges; first in the primary with 54.50% [S3][S7]

judicial.basis: Constitution as a broad framework applied with fidelity to purposes, broader state protections, Brennan's 'rights without remedies are hollow', and authorship of McCleary; her stated respect for text and structure keeps it at +1. Unchanged from the primary.

experience.basis: Eighteen years on the court, current Chief Justice, prior Court of Appeals service and the whole court's endorsement; unchanged from the primary.

measures.title: Initiative Measure No. IP26-645 concerns state and local taxes.
measures.what_it_does: Repeals the 9.9% tax on Washington taxable income above $1 million that the Legislature passed in 2026 (ESSB 6346), which would first apply to 2028 income, and adds a state law barring the state, counties, cities and all other local governments from taxing individual income or taxing by a measure of it. The sales tax, B&O tax and Working Families Tax Credit changes passed with the tax are not repealed.
measures.cost_line: OFM estimates $11.4 billion less state revenue over fiscal years 2027-2031, mostly from the general fund that pays for K-12, higher education and human services, including $377 million that would have gone to child care and early learning; agency savings of about $150 million; no effect on local revenue.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (State Sen. Chris Gildon, a retired Seattle firefighter/paramedic and small business owners) says voters have rejected an income tax ten times, that lawmakers left the door open to extend this one below $1 million, and that the Legislature has repeatedly shifted dedicated funds; it says the tax relief passed with the tax would stay in place.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Washington Education Association President Janie White, Washington State Labor Council President April Sims, a nurse, a teacher, a brewery owner and a Planned Parenthood Advocates representative) says the repeal is a tax break for the top 1% that would cut funding for schools, health care and childcare, and that the tax cuts for working families and small businesses depend on this revenue.

taxes.basis: YES repeals a 9.9% tax on income over $1 million (OFM: $11.4 billion in state revenue over SFY 2027-2031) and bars any future state or local income tax by statute: the rubric's 'limit & cut taxes' pole against its named 'millionaires tax' example of the other pole.

local-control.basis: YES writes one statewide rule that binds 'the state, counties, cities, and all other local jurisdictions', taking the income-tax option away from every local government (a state limit on local authority, the regional/state-standards pole). Strength 1, not 2: RCW 1.90.100 (I-2111) already bars local income taxes and ESSB 6346 left that ban in place for local governments, so the change for cities and counties is a re-enactment in broader terms.

spending.basis: The yes case rests on fiscal restraint and accountability (fund transfers, unkept spending commitments, 'demonstrate they can keep the commitments') while the no case and OFM tie the revenue to K-12, health care, childcare and free school meals; YES removes revenue the Legislature meant for those expansions. Strength 1 because the measure itself contains no audit or spending rule and the effect runs through revenue.

measures.title: Initiative Measure No. IL26-001 concerns parental rights relating to their children in public school.
measures.what_it_does: Restores the state's list of parents' rights in public schools (RCW 28A.605.005) to the version enacted by Initiative 2081 in 2024, undoing the Legislature's 2025 rewrite in ESHB 1296. Parents would get school records, including health and counseling records, within 10 business days instead of up to 45 days; prior notice when a school offers medical services; and wider opt-outs from surveys, assignments and activities. Several entries in the 2025 version (nondiscrimination, bullying complaints, enrollment, language access, special education) would leave the list, the nondiscrimination entry being replaced by an assurance against discrimination based on the family's religious beliefs, and records protection in abuse cases would narrow to medical, health and counseling records during an investigation of the parent.
measures.cost_line: OFM: no fiscal impact on state government and no effect on state or local revenue; school districts may have minor costs to update policies and procedures, amount indeterminate.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (two teachers who serve as union representatives, the La Center School District superintendent, a parent and education advocate, a women's rights advocate and a member of Democrats for an Informed Approach to Gender) says it restores parents' access to materials, records and medical notices, that safeguards for at-risk children should not become a default of withholding information from all parents, and that schools should not keep a child's new gender identity at school from parents.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (State Sen. John Lovick, the presidents of the Washington State Nurses Association and the League of Women Voters of Washington, a school counselor, and representatives of the state domestic violence coalition and Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates) says it would open sensitive records to parents under investigation for harming their child, weaken immediate notice when a child is a crime victim at school, and discourage students, including LGBTQ+ students, from seeking help from school staff.

parental-rights.basis: YES restores I-2081's notification, records and opt-out rights: copies of all student-specific records, including health and mental health counseling records, within 10 business days; prior notice of school-offered medical services; opt-outs from any survey, assignment or activity touching sexual experience, family beliefs or mental health; and removes the 'in accordance with policies and procedures' qualifier on curriculum access. That is the rubric's pole A ('Parental notification and opt-out', -2). The 2025 law it replaces kept FERPA's 45-day standard, chapter 70.02 RCW health-record confidentiality and federal-scope opt-outs, which is pole B. Strength 2: the measure's whole subject is this list, and nearly every change on notice, records and opt-outs moves toward pole A (the exception is crime notice, which moves from 'upon receipt of a report' to when a criminal action 'is deemed to have been committed', while dropping the on-campus limit); the entries it drops (enrollment, language access, special education, bullying complaints) are not notification or opt-out rights, and the AG says the 2025 list restated many rights found elsewhere in law.

measures.title: Initiative Measure No. IL26-638 concerns participation in athletics at K-12 schools.
measures.what_it_does: Requires school district and WIAA rules to bar students the measure calls "biologically male" from girls-only interschool competitions, individual or team, at public K-12 schools and private schools in the WIAA. Every student entering a girls-only competition would need a statement from her own health care provider, as part of the sports physical, verifying biological sex based on reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels. It replaces the current WIAA rule that students compete consistent with their gender identity.
measures.cost_line: OFM: about $21,000 one time for OSPI to update guidance; school districts may incur indeterminate costs to revise policies; no effect on state or local revenue. OFM does not estimate costs to families for verification.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (a coach, an Olympic medalist, a pediatrician, a student athlete, a parent and education advocate, and a member of Democrats for an Informed Approach to Gender) says it protects fairness in girls' sports and the rights established by Title IX, aligns Washington with federal law and international sports bodies, and that verification can happen during routine, non-invasive primary care.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (the presidents of the Washington State Nurses Association and the League of Women Voters of Washington, a family physician, a retired school nurse, a girls' wrestling coach and Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates) says it would subject girls, and only girls, to intrusive medical sex verification, burden families without a regular doctor, and bar the 5 to 10 transgender girls in school sports with no case-by-case decisions.

social.basis: YES writes sex-based eligibility into law for girls' interscholastic sports, with provider verification of biological sex for every girl entering a female-only competition, replacing WIAA Rule 18.16.0 (participation by gender identity). The rubric's social pole A (-2) names 'Sex-based eligibility for girls' and women's sports' and pole B names 'Trans participation in sports by gender identity'. Strength 2: this is the measure's only subject.
